s: Bankruptcy (uniform laws): includes a limited exception to state sovereign immunity (Katz).
Uniformity forbids private-debtor-specific laws (Railway Labor Executives' Ass'n v. Gibbons, 1982).
Naturalization: Congress has plenary authority over the rules for citizenship by naturalization, and broad immigration power as an incident of sovereignty (Chae Chan Ping, 1889).
Birthright citizenship flows from the Fourteenth Amendment's Citizenship Clause (Wong Kim Ark, 1898), not Article I.
Intellectual property: patents and copyrights "for limited Times" to "promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts."
Congress gets wide latitude on duration (Eldred v. Ashcroft, 2003, upholding the twenty-year copyright extension).
War and military powers: declaring war, raising armies, regulating the land and naval forces, calling forth the militia.
These support broad wartime economic regulation (Woods v. Cloyd W. Miller Co., 1948, rent control after the war) and military justice systems.
Treaty power: treaties may address matters beyond Article I, but must be construed to avoid displacing traditional state criminal law absent a clear statement (Bond v. United States, 2014).
Treaties cannot override constitutional rights (Reid v. Covert, 1957).
Property and territory: Congress may "make all needful Rules and Regulations respecting the Territory or other Property belonging to the United States" (Art. IV, § 3).
The Insular Cases doctrine governing unincorporated territories remains in force, though widely criticized.
Investigations: an implied power auxiliary to legislation, limited to valid legislative purposes.
Subpoenas for a President's personal records receive heightened scrutiny (Trump v. Mazars, 2020).
Federalism principles constrain even valid exercises of these powers.
Anti-commandeering and state sovereign immunity apply regardless of which power Congress invokes.
